findings: G1 core claim SUPPORTED: the source is the 2019 Nature study (s41586-019-1466-y) of a 'nationally representative sample of students in secondary education in the United States' and reports that a <1-hour online growth mindset intervention 'improved grades among lower-achieving students and increased overall enrolment to advanced mathematics courses' (growth-excerpts.txt line 14). Year, country, secondary-school population, and lower-achieving-student grade benefit all match the claim.

G1 context-dependence SUPPORTED at observational strength: abstract states 'the intervention changed grades when peer norms aligned with the messages of the intervention' (growth-excerpts.txt line 14); discussion states 'it was when the peer norm supported the adoption of intellectual challenges that the intervention promoted sustained benefits in the form of higher grades' (line 26).

G1 STRENGTH CAVEAT: the source explicitly limits causal interpretation of the context moderation — 'we cannot draw causal conclusions about the effects of the school norm, as the norms were measured, not manipulated' (growth-excerpts.txt line 27). The claim's wording 'effects depended on supportive school/peer context' is stronger than the source's correlational moderation; usable only if the measured-not-manipulated caveat travels with it.

G1 negative clause on university learners SUPPORTED: the study population is secondary-school adolescents, and the discussion states 'not all forms of growth mindset interventions can be expected to increase grades or advanced course-taking, even in the targeted subgroups' (growth-excerpts.txt line 28), so the source does not establish guaranteed effects for all learners, university or otherwise.

G1 neuroplasticity sub-clause NOT ANCHORED: the excerpt (abstract + discussion) contains no mention of neuroplasticity anywhere (growth-excerpts.txt lines 1-48). The negative statement 'does not establish that neuroplasticity alone proves intervention efficacy' is therefore not contradicted, but it is also not grounded in this source; it is an externally-safe hedge rather than an excerpt-supported finding.

H1 'approximate speculative framework' STRONGLY SUPPORTED: estimates given as 'approximately 50%... 10%... 40%' based on 'certain starting assumptions and a non-exhaustive review' (happiness-revisit.txt lines 41-44); authors say estimates were 'suggestions,' were 'approximate,'' derived from 'mere cross-sectional studies' (lines 126-128); 'we were speculative but not dogmatic' (line 20); 'scientific progress consists sometimes of engaging in speculation' (lines 136-142).

H1 'not a formula for partitioning one individual's happiness' ONLY INDIRECTLY SUPPORTED: the excerpt frames the percentages as population-level variance ('40% of the variance' lines 130-131; 'the variation in happiness' line 179) and as 'relative importance of the three factors in impacting chronic happiness levels' (lines 42-44); it never explicitly addresses individual-level application or warns against partitioning one person's happiness. Indirect inference is reasonable but the excerpt contains no direct statement.

H1 'later author revisit agrees with important critiques' SUPPORTED: 'the pie chart aspect of the model has received valid critiques. In this article, we start by agreeing with many such critiques' (happiness-revisit.txt lines 18-19); 'These critiques, with which we mostly agree' (lines 59-60).

H1 'acknowledges the activity estimate may overstate effects' STRONGLY SUPPORTED: 'Brown and Rohrer (2019) criticized our initial estimate that 40% of the variation in happiness is due to intentional activity. Based on our research of the last 15 years, we agree that this figure was likely an over-estimate' (happiness-revisit.txt lines 178-180); also 'such effects may be weaker than we initially believed' (line 23) and 'these effects tend to be smaller than we initially believed' (lines 89-90).

H1 publication metadata PARTIALLY UNSUPPORTED: online-2019 is evidenced — 'Published online: 07 Nov 2019' (happiness-revisit.txt line 7), citation '(2019)' and DOI 10.1080/17439760.2019.1689421 (lines 3-5), '© 2019 Informa UK Limited' (line 83). However, the 'journal2021' half of the distinction has NO evidence anywhere in the excerpt (lines 1-180 contain no 2021 date or journal-issue information); the excerpt is explicitly 'partial primary article only' (line 2), so the journal-issue year cannot be verified from this material.
